title: PPT-Eval: A Benchmark for Computer-Use Agents on PowerPoint Tasks
claim: Agents act on a task in a sandboxed environment, and rubric scoring gives graded partial credit with natural-language feedback on each outcome.
layout: Task and agent at top, four branching action trajectories fanning down to scored outputs
description: The figure opens at top left with a cartoon user and a speech bubble holding a task: add a fourth vCPU circle to slide 3 and to the time-sharing diagram. An arrow leads to a cluster of robot icons labeled Computer-Use Agents. A double-headed arrow links the agents to a PowerPoint Online screenshot labeled Sandboxed PowerPoint Online. Four colored trajectories fan out from the agents (red, orange, yellow, green). Each is a path of dots labeled with GUI actions such as scroll, key and click. Each path ends at a resulting slide thumbnail. Below each thumbnail is a rubric score (0, 0.18, 0.83, 1) and a quoted explanation in the matching color. The red result is a failure and the green result is a full success. The eye goes first to the speech bubble, then down the colored paths to the slides and scores.
caption: Illustration of task-solving in the \pptarena Benchmark. Given a task, an agent interacts with a file in a sandboxed instance of PowerPoint Online. Interaction can take full advantage of PowerPoint's feature-set using the GUI. \pptarena provides rubrics that can score different degrees of task completion and provide both nuanced partial credit and natural language feedback.
abstract: Creating and editing slides is a rich, multimodal activity that is ubiquitous in professional and educational settings, making it an ideal testbed for real-world computer-use agents. Microsoft PowerPoint is among the most widely adopted and feature-rich environments for presentation creation. We introduce PPT-Eval, a benchmark of 120 PowerPoint tasks across 12 files that cover both content creation and presentation editing scenarios, organized by difficulty. A central challenge in this domain is evaluation: tasks are complex, multimodal, and often admit many valid solutions. Moreover, today's agents frequently make only partial progress, which binary success metrics fail to capture. To address this, we design a robust evaluation framework to help create task-specific rubrics for PowerPoint tasks, taking inspiration from and building on past works for rubric-based evaluation. These rubrics award partial credit for intermediate steps, penalize unnecessary changes and poor aesthetics, and provide natural language feedback. This nuanced approach proves highly effective, achieving a Kendall's Ï-b correlation of 0.77 with human judgments. We find that existing frontier agents still struggle with solving PowerPoint tasks, with strong models like Claude-4.5-Opus achieving only a 45% success rate and an average partial score of 57%. The benchmark is located at: https://microsoft.github.io/ppteval.
